canonical_topic: LCOE as a fundamental-analysis upper bound on long-horizon power prices
definition: Levelized cost of entry (LCOE) is the break-even price a developer needs to justify building a new generating unit; it is used to estimate an equilibrium ceiling for electricity prices over very long forecast horizons.
core_idea: If market prices rise above LCOE, new generation becomes economic to build, and the resulting supply increase pushes prices back down, so LCOE functions as a supply-and-demand-based upper bound in long-term fundamental price forecasts.
key_points: Applies specifically to very long time horizons, not short-term price forecasting
Relies on a supply/demand feedback argument: price above LCOE incentivizes new build, which adds supply and caps price
In periods of continuously rising demand, new generation must be built, and its costs effectively set the market price
Calculated by spreading the cost of building a unit over its expected life, then dividing by expected generation volume to get a price per unit of output
relationships: Mathematically similar to annuity calculations used in finance/MBA coursework
trading_implications: Provides a long-horizon ceiling estimate useful for fundamental price forecasts
Used as a benchmark in PPA price negotiation and capacity market price estimation
caveats: LCOE is an approximation, not a precise price prediction — actual investment decisions are also shaped by project-specific technological and regional factors
